T1.name: Toyosu Market
T1.desc: Working wholesale market; tuna auction seen from upper windows
T1.why: Japan's biggest fish market at work; the dawn auction is free and calm that early.
T1.hours: Visitor areas ~5:00–17:00; tuna auction ~5:30–6:30. Closed Sun, holidays, most Wed (Nov 2026 closed 1, 3, 8, 11, 15, 18, 22, 23, 29). Open Thu 12.
T1.price: Free. No booking for the upper gallery.
T1.access: Taxi at dawn (trains start ~5:15): ask for Shijō-mae Station (市場前駅). Taxis can't drop at the market gates.
see: Tuna auction from the upper-floor glass gallery of the Fish Wholesale Market Building (Block 7). The floor is painted green so the red tuna meat stands out.
Panels in the gallery explain the bidding hand signals.
After the auction: buyers hauling tuna away, until ~7:00.
Restaurants on the upper floor of the market buildings for a light snack (queues form from ~7:00).

route.enter: Shijō-mae Station side, over the pedestrian walkway into the Fish Wholesale Market Building (Block 7).
walk: Follow the visitor signs to the upper-floor observation gallery above the tuna floor.
Watch the auction ~5:45–6:25, then the floor until ~7:00.
Optional: browse the Intermediate Wholesale Building (Block 6) and the restaurant area.
Light snack only (the Tsukiji tour includes food).
route.exit: Back via the walkway to Shijō-mae Station; taxi to Tsukiji (~15 min, ~¥1,500), leave ~7:45.

facts: Toyosu replaced the old Tsukiji inner market in 2018.
Visitors are never allowed on the market floor; only licensed buyers bid.
A lower observation deck closer to the floor is by lottery only (not possible for November).
tips: Arrive before 6:00: the best spots at the glass fill early.
It's cold at dawn in November: bring a layer.

T2.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
T2.desc: Old market site; food stalls, knife and tea shops
T2.why: The best place in Tokyo to graze on sushi, tamagoyaki and snacks.
T2.hours: Shops roughly 5:00/7:00–14:00, varies by shop. Closed Wed, Sun, holidays (follows the Toyosu calendar; closed Wed 11). Open Thu 12.
T2.price: Free; food per stall. Mostly cash.
T2.access: Hibiya Line Tsukiji Station, or Ōedo Line Tsukijishijō Station.
T2.booking: Guided tour booked Thu 12, 8:30–10:30 (Traveling Tokyo); food on the tour.
see: About 460 shops: tamagoyaki stands, grilled seafood, sushi counters.
Knife and tea shops in the side alleys.
Namiyoke Inari Shrine, the market's guardian shrine (founded 1659).
Tsukiji Hongwanji, a temple built in an ancient Indian style, next to the station.

route.enter: Meet 8:25 at the Starbucks in front of Tsukiji Station (Tsukiji 2-12-8).
walk: The guide leads through the main streets and the alleys behind them.
Eat at the stall where you buy; don't walk while eating.
Namiyoke Shrine is at the south-west edge of the market.
route.exit: Tour ends at the same Starbucks. Walk to Hamarikyū's Ōtemon Gate, 10–15 min.

facts: The inner (wholesale) market moved to Toyosu in 2018; the outer retail market stayed.
Namiyoke means 'protection from waves': the shrine was built when this land was reclaimed from the sea.
tips: Bring cash in small notes.
Ask before photographing shops.

T3.name: Tokyo National Museum
T3.why: Japan's top collection of swords, armour and prints; the Hiroshige show runs during our trip.
T3.hours: 9:30–17:00, last entry 16:30; Fri and Sat to 20:00. Closed Mon.
T3.price: Collection ¥1,000. Hiroshige ticket ¥1,500 includes the collection the same day (¥100 less online on Asoview, no booking needed).
T3.access: Ueno Park, 13-9 Ueno Kōen. JR Ueno Park exit, ~10 min walk.
see: Hiroshige: New Perspective on Edo Japan (29 Sep–20 Dec). 27 Oct–23 Nov shows the Kisokaidō series.
Honkan room 13 (1st floor, right side): Japanese swords, Heian to Edo periods.
Honkan rooms 5–6 (2nd floor): swords and armour of the military elite.
Honkan room 10 (2nd floor): ukiyo-e prints.

route.enter: Main gate on the Ueno Park side. Tickets at the gate booths.
walk: Straight ahead to the Honkan (the large main building).
Hiroshige exhibition first (check the signs for the room).
2nd floor: rooms 5–6 armour, room 10 prints.
1st floor: room 13 swords, last.
route.exit: Back out through the main gate, then through Ueno Park to JR Ueno (~10 min).

facts: Founded in 1872: Japan's oldest national museum.
The Honkan opened in 1938 and has 24 galleries on two floors.
The museum stands on land that belonged to Kan'ei-ji, the Tokugawa family temple.
The Hiroshige show celebrates a gift of 1,025 prints from the Uchiyama Susumu collection.
tips: Room numbers are on the floor plan at the entrance. Displays rotate, so a famous sword may not be out.

T4.name: Yanaka–Nezu
T4.why: One of the few old Tokyo areas that survived war and earthquakes; quiet, few tourists.
T4.hours: Nezu Shrine grounds 6:00–17:00 (seasonal); shrine office and goshuin 9:00–17:00. Yanaka streets 24 h; shops ~10:00–18:00.
T4.stay: 3 h tour + 30 min at Nezu Shrine
T4.access: JR Nippori, north ticket gate (tour meeting point).
T4.booking: Guided tour booked Wed 11, 10:30–13:30 (Localized), €56.30 for two.
see: Tennōji temple with its bronze Buddha from 1690.
Yanaka Cemetery: quiet lanes, grave of the last Tokugawa shogun.
Yūyake Dandan, the 'sunset steps' down to Yanaka Ginza.
Yanaka Ginza: about 70 small shops and snack stalls; cat motifs everywhere.
Nezu Shrine: lacquered halls from 1706 and the Otome Inari path of red torii gates.

route.enter: JR Nippori north ticket gate, 10:20 (next to NewDays).
walk: The tour route is the guide's; it ends at Yanaka Ginza around 13:30.
Lunch around Yanaka Ginza or on the way to Nezu.
Walk south ~20 min to Nezu Shrine: enter by the main torii, then the Otome Inari torii path on the left side of the main hall.
route.exit: From Nezu Shrine walk ~20–25 min via Ueno Sakuragi to the Tokyo National Museum.

facts: Nezu Shrine's present buildings were built in 1706 by the fifth Tokugawa shogun, Tsunayoshi.
The shrine claims a founding about 1,900 years ago, by the legendary prince Yamato Takeru.
Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the last shogun, is buried in Yanaka Cemetery.
tips: Narrow lanes with no sidewalks: watch for cars.
Keep voices low in the cemetery and residential lanes.

T5.name: Chanko-nabe dinner, Ryōgoku
T5.why: Hearty local dish in the sumo district.
T5.hours: Chanko Kawasaki: 17:00–21:00 (Sat to 20:30). Closed Sun and holidays (one listing also says Wed). Open Thu 12.
T5.price: Nadai chanko ¥3,130 per portion (tables order from 2 portions); course ¥5,240. Cash only.
T5.access: Chanko Kawasaki, Ryōgoku 2-13-1. JR Ryōgoku, ~5 min walk.
T5.booking: Not booking; decide on the day. Tel. +81 3 3631 2529. Backups: Kirishima, Ami, Chanko Dojo.
see: Nadai chanko: 'soppu-daki' style, chicken bones simmered into a light, clear broth with chicken, vegetables and tofu.
Tsukune (hand-made chicken meatballs) grilled or in the pot.
Finish with rice or noodles in the leftover broth (shime).
facts: Chanko Kawasaki opened in 1937, founded by the former wrestler Yokoteyama: Ryōgoku's oldest chanko shop.
'Chanko' means any meal eaten in a sumo stable; the hot pot is the famous one.
Chicken is traditional: it stands on two legs, like a wrestler who stays on his feet.
tips: Cash only.
No booking for 2 people: arrive at 17:00 opening to be safe.

route.enter: JR Ryōgoku west exit; the restaurant is right by the station (Ryōgoku 2-13-1).
walk: Small wooden house; take shoes off if seated on tatami.
Order the pot for two; the staff start it at the table.
Ryōgoku Kokugikan (sumo hall) is a 3-min walk if you want to see it from outside.
route.exit: Back to JR Ryōgoku, or Ōedo Line Ryōgoku (~5 min walk).

T6.name: Kappabashi
T6.desc: Kitchen-tool street: knives, ceramics, food samples
T6.why: A real working street for chefs, 5 min from the hotel.
T6.hours: Most shops 9:00/10:00–17:00/17:30; many closed Sun and holidays. Open Thu 12.
T6.stay: 40 min before the class + ~30 min after
T6.access: Tawaramachi Station (Ginza Line), ~5 min walk. The hotel is next to it.
see: Niimi: the giant chef's head on the roof at the south end.
Kama-Asa (since 1908): knives and iron pans; staff help you choose.
Kamata Hakensha (since 1923): knives and sharpening.
Ganso Shokuhin Sample-ya: realistic plastic food samples.
The golden Kappa statue at the Kappabashi crossing.

route.enter: South end, at the Niimi chef's head (Asakusa-dōri).
walk: Walk the whole ~800 m to the north end first without buying, to see all the shops.
Then come back to the shops you liked; the knife shops are mid-street.
Class at 15:00 at Nishiasakusa 1-9-8 (T10).
route.exit: Back to the south end; the hotel and Tawaramachi Station are 5 min away.

facts: About 170 shops line an 800 m street.
The street began trading second-hand kitchen tools around 1912.
A kappa is a water spirit; legend links it to a flood-control canal dug here.
tips: Knives go in checked baggage only.
Ask for tax-free with your passport (purchases over ¥5,000).

T7.name: Imperial Palace East Gardens
T7.why: Free walk through the stone walls of Ieyasu's (Toranaga's) castle; a core Shōgun site.
T7.hours: Closed Mon and Fri. Nov: 9:00–16:00 (last entry 15:30).
see: Stone walls and moats of Edo Castle.
Foundations of the main keep (tenshudai), a 1600s stone base.
Ninomaru garden.

route.enter: Ōtemon Gate (Ōtemachi Station).
walk: Up through the guardhouses to the Honmaru plateau and the keep base.
route.exit: Hirakawamon or Kitahanebashimon gate.

facts: Edo Castle's keep burned in 1657 and was never rebuilt.

T8.name: Shibamata
T8.desc: Old temple town; Taishakuten carvings, Edo River ferry
see: Taishakuten temple: wooden halls covered in fine carvings.
Taishakuten-sandō street: kusa-dango, eel, soba.
Yagiri no Watashi: hand-rowed ferry across the Edo River.

route.enter: Keisei Shibamata Station.
walk: Sandō street → Taishakuten → Suikei-en garden → Yagiri ferry.
route.exit: Back to Shibamata Station.

T9.name: Tochō observation deck
T9.desc: Free view from 202 m; Fuji on clear days
T9.why: Free big-city view, Fuji on a clear day.
T9.hours: South Deck 9:30–22:00 (last entry 21:30), closed 1st and 3rd Tue (Nov: 4 and 17). North Deck 9:30–17:30, closed 2nd and 4th Mon (Nov: 9 and 24). Both open Fri 13.
T9.access: Tochōmae Station (Ōedo Line), direct. ~10 min walk from Shinjuku Station west exit.
see: 360° view over Tokyo from the 45th floor.
Skytree to the east, Fuji to the west on clear days (best before sunset).

route.enter: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building No. 1, 1st floor: follow the signs to the observatory lifts. Bag check before the lift.
walk: Lift to the 45th floor.
Walk the full circle; Fuji is on the west side.
route.exit: Same lift down. Unatetsu in Kabukichō is ~20 min on foot.

facts: The twin-tower building (1991) was designed by Kenzō Tange.

T10.name: Fuji Japan sharpening class
T10.why: Learn to sharpen a Japanese knife properly, next to Kappabashi.
T10.access: 1-9-8 Nishiasakusa, Taitō-ku (Fujijapan sign at the entrance), a few minutes' walk from the hotel.
T10.booking: Viator ref 1462063611 (operator VIA-108304929), booked via Expedia 73580595256490. Tel. +81 3 6824 5991.
see: Whetstone grits (coarse → fine) and how to hold the angle.
Hands-on practice on a Japanese knife under guidance; all tools provided.
Tips for care at home: drying, storage, when to re-sharpen.
tips: Come empty-handed: knife, whetstone, stand, apron and towel are provided.
Knife shops on Kappabashi give a free first sharpening on purchase.

route.enter: Look for the Fujijapan sign at 1-9-8 Nishiasakusa; arrive 5–10 min early (15:00 start).
walk: 2 h session; ends back at the meeting point.
route.exit: Kappabashi is next door; most shops close 17:00–17:30.

facts: Japanese knives are usually sharpened at a narrower angle (~15°) than Western ones (~20°).
Many Japanese knives are single-bevel: sharpened on one side only.

T11.name: Mt. Takao
T11.why: Easy forest hike with a mountain temple and autumn colour; Tokyo's nature day.
T11.decision: Fri 13 Option A, if the weather is good (decide Thu evening)
T11.hours: Cable car 8:00–17:45 in November (every 15 min); chairlift 9:00–16:30. Yakuōin grounds open daytime.
T11.access: Keio Line Shinjuku → Takaosanguchi, ~50 min. Not JR Takao Station.
see: Yakuōin: mountain temple with tengu (long-nosed goblin) statues. 📿 stamp.
Takosugi: a giant cedar with octopus-like roots on Trail 1.
Summit (599 m): view over Tokyo; Fuji on clear mornings.
Autumn colour: summit mid–late November, lower slopes later.

route.enter: Takaosanguchi Station → Kiyotaki Station (cable car), ~5 min walk.
walk: Cable car up (~6 min) or walk Trail 1 from the bottom (3.8 km, ~100 min up).
Trail 1 (paved) from the upper station past Takosugi to Yakuōin.
Continue on Trail 1 to the summit (~40–60 min from the upper station).
Soba lunch near the summit or on the way down.
route.exit: Down by Trail 1 or the cable car; Keio Line back to Shinjuku.

facts: The cable car climbs at about 31°, one of the steepest in Japan.
Yakuōin was founded in 744, a centre of mountain worship.
tips: Start early: autumn queues at the cable car build after 9:00.
Trail 1 is paved; other trails are real mountain paths.

T12.name: Edo-Tokyo Museum
T12.desc: Edo life dioramas, Edo Castle model
T12.why: Best indoor overview of Edo life; a good rain backup.
see: Life-size half of Nihonbashi bridge.
Models of Edo Castle and townhouses.

route.enter: Ryōgoku Station (Ōedo Line A3/A4, 1 min).
walk: Permanent exhibition on 5F and 6F.
route.exit: Japanese Sword Museum next door.

facts: Reopened 31 Mar 2026 after renovation.
The building is the same height as the old Edo Castle keep.

T13.name: Sensō-ji
T13.desc: Oldest temple in Tokyo; early morning or evening only
T13.why: Iconic but crowded; only worth it at dawn or at night.
T13.decision: Optional: evening, if dinner is in Asakusa
T13.hours: Grounds 24 h. Lit from sunset to ~23:00; main hall closed at night. Nakamise shops from 10:00.
T13.access: Asakusa Station (Ginza Line); ~10 min walk from the hotel.
see: Kaminarimon (Thunder Gate) with its huge red lantern.
Nakamise street (shutters closed at night, painted with Edo scenes).
Hōzōmon gate and the five-storey pagoda, both lit at night.
Main hall from outside, with Skytree behind.

route.enter: Kaminarimon Gate on Kaminarimon-dōri.
walk: Straight along Nakamise to Hōzōmon.
Main hall courtyard; pagoda on the left.
route.exit: West side towards Kappabashi; the hotel is ~10 min walk.

facts: The temple claims a founding in 628.
The night lighting started in 2003, for Edo's 400th anniversary.
The pagoda was rebuilt in 1973; its top holds relics of the Buddha from Sri Lanka.

T14.name: Japanese Sword Museum
T14.desc: Blades; Old Yasuda Garden in front
see: Special exhibition 'Kotetsu and Sukehiro' (24 Oct–20 Dec 2026).
Old Yasuda Garden in front.

route.enter: Ryōgoku Station, next to the Edo-Tokyo Museum.
walk: One floor of displays; ~1 h.
route.exit: Through Old Yasuda Garden.

T15.name: Anjin-chō plaque
see: A small stone marker for the site of William Adams' Edo house, in a quiet side street.

route.enter: Mitsukoshimae Station (Ginza Line), exit towards Muromachi 1-chōme.
walk: Walk 2–3 min east of Mitsukoshi to the plaque (三浦按針屋敷跡).
route.exit: Back to Mitsukoshi for the depachika (T20).

facts: The street was called Anjin-chō from Adams' Japanese name, Miura Anjin.

T16.name: Kawagoe "Little Edo"
T16.why: Edo-era merchant town, but costs half a day.
see: Kurazukuri Street: clay-walled Edo warehouses.
Toki-no-Kane bell tower.
Kashiya Yokochō sweets alley.
Kita-in: Edo Castle rooms and 540 rakan statues.

route.enter: Tobu Kawagoe or Seibu Hon-Kawagoe Station.
walk: Walk north ~15–20 min to Ichibangai, then Kita-in.
route.exit: Bus or walk back to the station.

T18.name: Tsukishima monja
T18.why: A dish you only find in Tokyo, in an old shitamachi area.
T18.decision: Option B lunch, choice on the day
T18.hours: Many 11:00–23:00; some evening-only or closed Mon. Shorter queues at lunch.
T18.access: Tsukishima Station exit 7 (Ōedo/Yūrakuchō Line); ~30 min from the hotel.
see: Monjayaki: thin batter with cabbage and fillings (mentaiko-mochi-cheese is the classic), cooked on the table griddle.
Okonomiyaki is also on every menu if you prefer something firmer.
tips: Eat it straight off the griddle with the tiny spatula (hagashi).

route.enter: Tsukishima Station exit 7 (Ōedo/Yūrakuchō Line).
walk: Nishinaka-dōri, the 'Monja Street', starts at the exit; ~80 shops on both sides.
Pick a shop with a short queue; most have picture menus.
route.exit: Tsukishima Station; Tsukiji is 1 stop away.

facts: Tsukishima is land reclaimed from Tokyo Bay in 1892.
Monja began as a cheap snack for children in Tokyo's old downtown.

T19.name: Yūrakuchō gādo-shita
T19.desc: Yakitori and izakaya under railway arches
T19.why: Local post-war eating alleys, not built for tourists; evenings only.
T19.decision: Option B evening, choice on the day
T19.access: JR Yūrakuchō, or Ginza Line to Ginza (~20 min from the hotel).
see: Yakitori and beer under ~700 m of brick railway arches, trains rumbling overhead.
facts: Eating under the tracks began here in the black markets after WWII.
T19.hours: Most places from ~16:00/17:00 to late; some closed Sun.

route.enter: JR Yūrakuchō Station, Hibiya exit side.
walk: Walk along the brick arches between Yūrakuchō and Shimbashi.
Pick a busy yakitori stall; plastic stools and beer crates are normal.
route.exit: Yūrakuchō or Ginza Station (Ginza Line direct to Tawaramachi).

tips: Some places charge a small table charge (otōshi) with a starter.

T20.name: Depachika lunch
T20.why: Cheap tasting lunch with no extra travel, next to the Anjin-chō plaque.
T20.decision: Option B lunch, choice on the day
T20.hours: Mitsukoshi Nihombashi 10:00–19:00; basement food floor and 1F to 19:30.
T20.access: Mitsukoshi Nihombashi, Mitsukoshimae Station (Ginza Line, direct from Tawaramachi).
see: Basement food hall: bentō, sushi, wagashi sweets, perfect fruit.
The main hall on 1F: a 5-storey art-deco atrium with a huge Tennyo (Goddess) statue.
facts: The main building (1935) is an Important Cultural Property.
Mitsukoshi declared itself Japan's first department store in 1904.

route.enter: Mitsukoshimae Station (Ginza Line): exits lead straight into the store's basement.
walk: Food floor B1 (main and new buildings).
Eat-in corners are few: buy and eat in the rest area or at a counter.
route.exit: Anjin-chō plaque (T15) is 2–3 min away.

T21.name: Tempura and soba
T21.why: Only a meal, no extra time needed.
T21.decision: Option B lunch, choice on the day; no fixed place
T21.pending: No restaurant chosen yet: choose on the day.
see: Tempura: seafood and vegetables fried in light batter, eaten at a counter as they come out.
Soba: buckwheat noodles, cold (zaru) with dipping sauce or hot in broth.
facts: Both were Edo fast food, sold from street stalls in the 1700s.
tips: Slurping soba is normal and polite.

T22.name: Shinjuku Unatetsu
T22.desc: Eel only: skewers of every part, unajū, hitsumabushi
T22.why: Your pick: the whole eel, head to tail, grilled on skewers.
T22.hours: 11:00–23:30 (last order 23:00), daily; closed 31 Dec–2 Jan. (Ikyu lists 11:00–24:30.)
T22.access: Unatetsu Hanare, Kabukichō 1-22-2. Seibu-Shinjuku Stn 1 min, JR Shinjuku east exit 5 min; ~35 min from the hotel.
T22.booking: To book: Ikyu restaurant.ikyu.com/117045 (Japanese, use Chrome translate; 100% cancellation fee). Fri 13, 16:30, 2 people.
see: The skewer set: liver (kimo), fins (hire), belly (bara), head (kabuto) and more, each grilled differently.
Unajū: grilled eel on rice in a lacquer box.
Hitsumabushi: eat it three ways (plain, with condiments, then with broth).
tips: Cards and PayPay accepted. Non-smoking (heated tobacco on 3F only).

route.enter: Kabukichō 1-22-2: a small two-storey house; Seibu-Shinjuku Station 1–2 min.
walk: Counter on 1F (watch the grilling), tatami room on 2F.
Order the skewer set plus one unajū or hitsumabushi to share.
route.exit: Seibu-Shinjuku / JR Shinjuku east exit; ~35 min to the hotel.

facts: Unatetsu started in 1962 in Shibuya (the original is T25).
The eel is grilled directly over charcoal without steaming (Kansai style).

T23.name: Tama Sushi, Kanda
T23.why: Your pick: a neighbourhood sushi counter, not a tourist place.
T23.hours: ⚠️ Unclear: one 2026 listing shows lunch only (Mon–Fri 11:00–15:00, closed Sat, Sun, holidays); older listings and reviews show dinner too. Confirm by phone on Tue 10.
T23.price: Lunch nigiri ~¥1,100; dinner budget ¥2,000–8,000 depending on listing.
T23.access: Kanda Tsukasamachi 2-16-8. Shin-Ochanomizu / Awajichō / Ogawamachi Stn, 3 min.
T23.booking: Phone only: +81 3 3256 3220. Ask APA reception on Tue 10 to call.
see: Edomae nigiri served one piece at a time by the chef.
Ask for omakase (chef's choice).
tips: Solo chef: service is slow, relax.
Smoking used to be allowed (check).

route.enter: Kanda Tsukasamachi 2-16-8, on Ichihachi-dōri; Awajichō Station exit A2, ~3 min.
walk: Counter of 6–8 seats; sit at the counter.
route.exit: Ginza Line from Kanda or Awajichō area back to Tawaramachi (~12 min).

facts: The shop has been on this street for over 40 years.
Neighbour: Yatsude-ya, a famous old tendon (tempura rice bowl) shop.

T24.name: Sushi Mitsuyoshi, Shinjuku Gyoen
T24.why: Chef-chosen omakase with sake at a fair price.
T24.decision: Over 1 h travel for one meal; replaced by T24a, T24b or T24c
see: 8-seat counter, omakase of 22 items with optional sake pairing.
T24.hours: Dinner from 17:00 (last seating 20:00); closed Sun and holidays.

T24a.name: Sushi Kajiwara, Nezu
T24a.desc: Neighbourhood sushi counter near the end of T4
T24a.why: Least extra travel on the Yanaka–Nezu day.
T24a.decision: Backup dinner, choice on the spot
T24a.hours: Lunch 11:30–12:30, dinner 17:30–21:00; closed Sun and Mon (user listing, not confirmed online on 6 Nov).
T24a.access: Nezu 2-30-2, Bunkyō-ku. Nezu Stn 4 min. Tel. 03-5685-0933.
see: Small counter sushi in a residential street near Nezu Shrine.

route.enter: Nezu Station (Chiyoda Line), 4 min.
walk: Counter seats; ask for omakase.
route.exit: Nezu Station → Chiyoda Line.

facts: Nezu, Yanaka and Sendagi together are nicknamed 'Yanesen'.

T24b.name: Sushi Kanesho, Asakusa
T24b.why: Closest match to Mitsuyoshi's counter and sake.
T24b.decision: Backup dinner, choice on the spot
T24b.hours: Dinner Tue–Sat 17:00–22:00 (L.O. 21:00), Sun and holidays 17:00–21:00; lunch Wed–Sun 11:30–14:00. Closed Mon and 1st and 3rd Sun. Open Wed 11.
T24b.access: Asakusa 3-33-9. Tsukuba Express Asakusa exit A2, 9 min. Tel. 03-3871-6081.
T24b.booking: Book on Ikyu; 100% fee for cancellations or changes.
see: 8–9-seat counter with chef's omakase; seasonal fish and sake chosen to match.

route.enter: Asakusa 3-33-9, Miyashita Bldg 101; north of Sensō-ji.
walk: Counter seating; course only.
route.exit: ~15 min walk to the hotel, or taxi.

facts: Listed as a Michelin Guide Tokyo Selected restaurant (2024 and 2026).

T24c.name: Sushi Yu, Asakusa
T24c.desc: Edomae sushi with raw bluefin, near the hotel
T24c.why: Close to the hotel, but dinner starts at 18:00.
T24c.decision: Backup dinner, choice on the spot
T24c.hours: Mon–Sat 18:00–22:30 (L.O. 22:00); closed Sun and holidays. Reservation only, at least 3 days ahead. Open Wed 11.
T24c.access: Nishi-Asakusa 3-16-8. Tsukuba Express Asakusa exit A2, 1 min; Tawaramachi Stn 7 min. Tel. 03-3845-1913.
T24c.booking: Hot Pepper; online booking closes 3 days before at 18:00.
see: Edomae sushi with raw (never frozen) wild bluefin and aged white fish.
Counter with 'hand-passed' nigiri, plus 2 private rooms.

route.enter: Nishi-Asakusa 3-16-8; Tsukuba Express Asakusa exit A2, 1 min.
walk: Sit at the counter for the hand-passed nigiri.
route.exit: ~7 min walk to the hotel.

facts: The owner trained at Ginza Sushi-kō, founded 1885.

T25.name: Ganso Unatetsu, Shibuya
T25.why: A second eel meal only if we pass through Shibuya.
see: The original Unatetsu: skewers of every eel part at dinner.
T25.hours: Mon–Thu 11:30–15:00 and 16:30–22:30, Fri to 23:00, Sat 16:30–21:00; closed Sun and holidays.

T26.name: Shunkaen Bonsai Museum
T26.desc: Master Kunio Kobayashi's garden; optional workshop
see: Bonsai master Kunio Kobayashi's garden, hundreds of trees, some centuries old.
Optional 1 h workshop.

T27.name: Hamarikyū Gardens + Nakajima no Ochaya
T27.desc: Tokugawa shogun garden, tidal pond, teahouse on the water
T27.why: Old shogunal garden 10–15 min walk from Tsukiji, with a calm matcha break in the pond teahouse; not a ceremony.
T27.access: From Tsukiji walk 10–15 min to Ōtemon Gate (north). Shiodome Station is nearest to Naka-no-gomon Gate.
see: The 300-year pine just inside Ōtemon: planted in 1709 by the 6th shogun, Ienobu.
Shioiri-no-ike: a tidal pond fed by seawater from Tokyo Bay.
Nakajima no Ochaya: the teahouse on an island in the pond, with Shiodome towers behind.
Duck-hunting blinds (kamoba) used by the shoguns.

route.enter: Ōtemon Gate (north side, Tsukiji side). Tickets at the gate.
walk: Pine tree on the left just inside the gate.
Follow the paths south to the tidal pond.
Cross the long wooden bridge to Nakajima no Ochaya: matcha and sweet (~30 min).
Best photo of the teahouse from the bridge.
route.exit: Back out through Ōtemon, then walk ~15 min to Ginza (T28).

facts: Built as a lord's residence in 1654, later a shogun's villa, then an imperial detached palace.
There were five teahouses; all were lost in the 1923 earthquake or WWII. Nakajima was rebuilt in 1983.
The Asakusa water bus to the garden has been suspended since April 2026.
tips: Mid-November colour is still early: come for the garden and the teahouse.

T28.name: Ginza
T28.desc: Department stores, food halls, regional shops
T28.why: Two shops worth the stop on one short walk after Tsukiji: Ishikawa (regional goods) and Itoya (stationery).
T28.hours: Itoya: Mon–Sat 10:00–20:00, Sun and holidays 10:00–19:00. Ishikawa shop: 10:30–20:00, closed only at New Year (older listing, verify).
T28.access: ~15 min walk from Hamarikyū/Tsukiji. Back: Ginza Line direct to Tawaramachi, ~18 min.
see: Ishikawa shop (いしかわ百万石物語・江戸本店, Ginza 2-2-18): Ishikawa Prefecture goods; ask for the Agehama salt.
Itoya (Ginza 2-7-15): a 12-floor stationery store with a red paperclip sign.

route.enter: From Hamarikyū walk north-west to Ginza.
walk: Itoya on Chūō-dōri (2-7-15).
Ishikawa shop a short walk north-east (2-2-18).
route.exit: Ginza Station → Ginza Line direct to Tawaramachi (~18 min).

facts: Ginza is named after the silver mint the shogunate set up here in 1612.

H1.name: Kamata winged gyoza
H1.why: The local dish of our last night, 4 min by train from Kc-III.
H1.access: Nihao annex: Kamata 4-25-7, basement; Keikyū Kamata east exit ~3 min. Ōtorii → Keikyū Kamata 4 min.
H1.booking: No booking needed (busy at 19:00: go at 18:30).
see: Hanetsuki gyoza with the crispy 'wing' of batter.
Steamed and boiled gyoza to compare.
facts: Nihao's founder, Yagi Isao, from Dalian, opened in Kamata in 1983 and created the winged gyoza, inspired by Shanghai fried buns.
Kangei (歓迎), Kamata's other classic, was opened by his relatives.
tips: Ask for the vinegar-and-pepper dip: a local habit.
